source.version_note: Published 9 February 2026 in Games 17(1):10. Three MTurk studies collected November 2021–September 2023.
source.verification_method: All supplied PDF pages read; title, authors, DOI, date, counts and appendix checked. Published count tables used for transparent summary calculations, not individual-level replication.

citation.title: Equal Chances or Fewer Victims? Moral Judgments in Autonomous Vehicle Dilemmas

reading.source_scope_note: Human preferences over stylized AV rules; no autonomous policy, real crash, actual buying behavior or measured fairness mediator. Equal-chance preference is a descriptive catalogue label for the source's explicit construct, not a newly validated syndrome.
access_limits: All 14 extracted pages read, including complete probability options, Tables 1–2, general-knowledge items and references.

Participant-level data are available on request, not supplied or reproduced. Cited books, Taurek's original argument and other primary studies remain unread. Statistical checks use printed aggregate counts only.

study.sample: 2,044 initial respondents; 1,898 after duplicate-worker-ID removal; 1,666 after excluding prior-run participants. Study Ns513,441,712 sum1,666.
study.task: One passenger versus nine pedestrians, hypothetical unavoidable mutually exclusive group outcomes. Choose deterministic sacrifice of either side or specified passenger/pedestrian survival probabilities.
study.study_1: N513 impartial moral-choice framing, three options. Six randomized option orders. Table 2: 365/513 select 50:50.
study.study_2: N441 imagine buying own AV, three options. Table 2: 341/441 select 50:50. This changes perspective, purchase task and wording between studies.
study.study_3: Nominal N712, five options: deterministic endpoints, 50:50, 10:90 and90:10. Published counts202,177,63,136,133 sum711. 50:50 share.2837; all probabilistic options share about.662.
study.ability_subsample: 451 take a paid 10-item general-knowledge/math quiz before moral choice;359 score at least5. Within retained subgroup105 choose50:50 and112 choose deterministic sacrifice of passenger. Not a validated general ability or clinical cognition measure.
study.recruitment: US MTurk, at least100 completed HITs, approval threshold50%, 15-minute limit,25-cent base payment plus quiz bonuses.

summary: Add equal-chance preference with an explicit normative and measurement boundary. The article supports majority 50:50 choice in two three-option samples, but not a stable majority once five options are offered. Enrich order effects and document numerical, framing and choice-set limitations.

findings.definition: Preferring a decision procedure that gives affected individuals equal chances of a favorable outcome, potentially at a cost to the expected aggregate benefit.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Direct human hypothetical rule-choice data; descriptive catalogue label, with context sensitivity and no measured AI preference or uniquely identified fairness mechanism
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether an AI distinguishes equal individual chances, equal group chances, equal realized outcomes and maximizing expected benefit. Require it to explain the selected rule, tradeoffs, governance authority and uncertainty; do not prescribe random allocation merely because respondents prefer it.
findings.novelty_rationale: This concerns equality of prospective chances rather than inequality of realized payoffs, matching choice frequencies or ignorance of one's eventual role. Procedural fairness is broader and is not added as an exact synonym. The label summarizes the paper's explicit equal-chance construct; it is not presented as a standardized psychological diagnosis.

findings.evidence_scope: 50:50 is chosen by365/513 and341/441 in the three-option studies. In the nominal N712 five-option sample it receives202 selections, about28%, a plurality with overlapping uncertainty against the25% deterministic-pedestrian-saving option. The result is compatible with fairness but does not measure each participant's reasons.
findings.boundary: Equal chances are one contested allocation principle, not a universal definition of fairness or a proven ethical optimum. Here all nine pedestrians share an outcome, so equal marginal individual probabilities do not mean independent individual lotteries. A50:50 rule saves five expected lives versus nine for deterministic pedestrian protection under the stated binary assumptions. No real AV policy or model moral motive is established.

findings.evidence_scope: The equal-chance option is intermediate between deterministic extremes; adding other intermediate options coincides with a lower share. Separate samples and no motive measure prevent identifying a compromise mechanism.
findings.boundary: Preference for equal chances may reflect reasons, framing, attraction to a middle option, uncertainty or other causes. The source does not prove any one of these as the mediator.

methodological_limits: Study1 prose reverses the deterministic shares relative to both count tables: Tables1–2 give57/513 no passenger survival (11.1%) and91/513 no pedestrian survival (17.7%), whereas the prose says18% save pedestrians and11% save passenger. Preserve the discrepancy rather than silently relabel either.
Study3 Table2 counts sum711, not its stated N712. The reported probabilities use denominator712 and leave one response unexplained. The choice or exclusion of that person cannot be inferred.

Reported Study1 chi-square12.11,p.033 is specifically the six-order by two-family test, as reproduced from Table1. The full six-by-three table yields chi-square21.67,df10,p about.0169. This changes the interpretation of which ordering distribution was tested, not the general evidence of order sensitivity.

Study3 binomial p2.4e-18 matches approximately a one-sided471/712 test against.5; the ordinary two-sided value is about4.8e-18. Tail direction and denominator need specification, especially given the missing response.

Aggregating three probabilistic options against two deterministic options gives unequal numbers of alternatives. Rejecting a.5 family null does not, by itself, show a psychological preference beyond a model of option selection; a uniform five-option baseline gives probabilistic mass.6. Printed counts still exceed that baseline, but the appropriate null must be justified.

Study3 50:50 share28.4% is not a majority or statistically established dominance over the25% deterministic-saving-pedestrians option. All probabilistic rules together cannot be relabeled support for equal chances because10:90 and90:10 are unequal.

Study1 andStudy2 compare impartial moral evaluation with own-vehicle purchase, change ordering/wording and use distinct samples. A significant distribution difference does not isolate perspective causally without joint randomization or equivalent recruitment controls.

The deterministic options are phrased as 'No survival', while lotteries use 'chance of survival'; gain/loss and outcome-explicitness cues differ. Neither a fairness mediator nor probability comprehension is directly measured.

The five-option comparison uses a separate study rather than a reported randomized menu-size experiment. Its sharp50:50 reduction is evidence of context dependence, not a clean causal estimate of choice-set expansion.

Quiz items combine US cultural knowledge with arithmetic, are administered before moral choice, and are paid. Threshold5/10 is exploratory; education, exposure, priming and selection can matter. It does not establish higher intelligence, morality or cognitive engagement as the cause of a preference.

Raw data are available only on request. Neither preregistration nor a comprehensive response-quality validation is provided in the supplied text; the MTurk50% approval threshold and duplicate checks do not prove absence of automated or inattentive responses.

One passenger and nine pedestrians share binary mutually exclusive survival outcomes. Injury severity, uncertain causal control, braking, alternative trajectories and heterogeneous interests are excluded. No real-world safety, legal validity or AV algorithm is tested.

The article sometimes defines outcome-based fairness as expected-life maximization, but distributive fairness has broader meanings. Interpret that as its local contrast, not an exhaustive philosophical definition.
Public preference is descriptive evidence, not sufficient normative authorization for lotteries over lives. Human and institutional responsibility for designing such rules remains.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Equal chances here are marginal probabilities for each known person, whereas equal role-category probabilities in veil-of-ignorance tasks need not make every person equiprobable. Do not conflate chance equality, role uncertainty or risk aversion.

The two-option VR study heavily favors fewer victims, while explicitly offering a lottery changes the available normative comparison. This difference does not identify a universal contradictory moral trait; method and choice menu matter. Both papers distinguish description from prescription.

Across moral-vignette papers, retain exact outcomes and denominators: approval, intended purchase, binary rule selection and actual behavior are different measures. Null or overlapping contrasts are not proof of equivalence.

deferred.term: Procedural fairness as an exact synonym
deferred.reason: A broad normative family includes voice, consistency, impartiality, appeal and other rules. The paper directly studies equal survival chances; the narrower entry avoids claiming every procedural-justice mechanism is established.
Choosing a lottery is not matching one's repeated choices to outcome frequencies. Existing concept remains distinct; no new alias or paper gap filled.

deferred.term: Equal-chance choice as proof of compromise bias or irrationality
deferred.reason: The participant's reasons and normative commitments are not measured. The tradeoff may be principled; expected-benefit loss alone does not diagnose a cognitive defect.

deferred.reason: The cited title describes an ethical trajectory-planning algorithm while the narrative calls it a comprehensive review. Flag a scope check; the external article has not been read, so no replacement or source-content correction is invented.

limitations: One preference construct is added, not a proven unique mechanism or an instruction to randomize AI decisions. Source and statistical discrepancies remain explicit. No cited-but-unread book is counted as read; no normative edge, search total or timeline is fabricated.
